$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot (-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$

We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions.

Let $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write $$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}].$$

Recall that, under this notation,

- $\mathbf u = [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]$ represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and
- $\mathbf x = [\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]$ represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

$$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = \mathbf{T}\left( [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \right) = [\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}v \\ u\operatorname{sin}v\end{aligned}]$$

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/dc/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and
- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms." :tutorial/id #uuid "c831da3f-8fff-5c5b-8be5-f3602a7303ba" {:db/id 17592186130231 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130466 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

$$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}].$$

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}$$

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

$$[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] = \mathbf{T}\left( [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \right) = [\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}v \\ u\operatorname{sin}v\end{aligned}]$$

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}v & -u\operatorname{sin}v \\ \operatorname{sin}v & u\operatorname{cos}v\end{aligned}| \\ & =\operatorname{cos}v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}v \\ & =u{cos}^{2}v+u{sin}^{2}v \\ & =u({cos}^{2}v+{sin}^{2}v) \\ & =u.\end{aligned}$$

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "c956f456-bd29-5cf7-83bd-de9b757b718f" :step/math-academy-id 44557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130233}} {:db/id 17592186130233 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130468 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones.

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where $$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]$$

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson).

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$.

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).
- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)< 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)
- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones.

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where $$\mathbf{T}: [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}] \longrightarrow [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]$$

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson).

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$.

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).
- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)< 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)
- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7673 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "0e6a94d3-c32f-5582-98ea-69a8605ef653" :step/math-academy-id 44558 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130236}} {:db/id 17592186130468 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.
